issues.legal_issue: A restriction imposed by a testamentary disposition made after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act remains effective when the female beneficiary acquires no pre-existing right in the property.
material_facts: The property was the testator’s self-acquired property.

The testator’s will gave his widow an interest in the property subject to restrictions, including that the property would pass to other beneficiaries on her death and that she could not sell or mortgage it during her lifetime.
The widow acquired the property under the will after the Hindu Succession Act had commenced; she was not in possession of it when the Act commenced.
Apart from the will, the widow had a right to maintenance, but no charge over the testator’s separate property had been created.
The lower appellate court found the will genuine and duly executed, and the High Court proceeded on the basis that the property came to the widow under that will.
issues.conclusion: The widow’s interest was governed by the restrictions in the will. Section 14(1) did not enlarge it into an absolute estate; Section 14(2) applied.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, Section 14(1) applies where a female Hindu possessed property at the commencement of the Act under a semblance of a right, including a pre-existing right; Section 14(2) applies to a later instrument that creates a new restricted interest. A right to maintenance, without a charge or other right in the property, does not itself give a widow a pre-existing right in her husband’s separate property. Section 30 permits a Hindu to dispose of property by will, and a beneficiary takes subject to valid terms of that will. The Court distinguished V. Tulasamma v. V. Shesha Reddi and Raghubar Singh v. Gulab Singh, and relied on Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva, Eramma v. Verrupanna, Dindyal v. Rajaram, Mst. Karmi v. Amru, Bhura v. Kashi Ram and Sharad Subramanyan v. Soumi Mazumdar.

rule.if: testamentary_succession_dispute and separate_property and beneficiary_acquired_interest_after_act_commencement and will_imposes_restriction and no_preexisting_right_in_property

predicates.testamentary_succession_dispute: The dispute concerns the interest a female beneficiary acquired under a will.
predicates.separate_property: The testator owned the property separately rather than as part of a joint family estate.
predicates.beneficiary_acquired_interest_after_act_: The female beneficiary acquired her interest under the will after the relevant succession law had commenced.
predicates.will_imposes_restriction: The will limits the beneficiary’s interest or restricts her dealings with the property.
predicates.no_preexisting_right_in_property: The beneficiary had no pre-existing right in the property itself, even if she had a claim to maintenance.

issues.definition: When a female beneficiary receives separate property under a will after the succession law has commenced, and she had no pre-existing right in the property, a restriction imposed by the will remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: An apparently absolute testamentary gift is limited to a life interest when that construction reconciles it with the will’s provisions giving the property to others after the first beneficiary’s death.
material_facts: The will described the widow as owner of the property during her lifetime.
It also provided that two other beneficiaries would take the property after her death.
The will prohibited the widow from transferring the property by will to other heirs and separately stated that she could not sell or mortgage it during her lifetime.
issues.conclusion: Read as a whole, the will gave the widow a life estate, not an absolute estate.
issues.legal_principle: A court should, so far as legally possible, give effect to every disposition in a will and harmonize its provisions. Where a gift appears absolute but a successive gift is made to take effect on the first beneficiary’s death, the first interest may be construed as a life interest to give effect to both dispositions. If repugnant provisions cannot be reconciled, the later provision may prevail. The Court relied on Ramchandra Shenoy v. Mrs. Hilda Brite.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and apparently_absolute_gift and successive_gift_after_first_beneficiary_death and restrictions_support_limited_interest

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The court must determine the extent of an interest created by a will.
predicates.apparently_absolute_gift: The will uses language that, read alone, appears to give the first beneficiary an absolute interest.
predicates.successive_gift_after_first_beneficiary_: The will gives the same property to another beneficiary after the first beneficiary dies.
predicates.restrictions_support_limited_interest: Other terms of the will restrict the first beneficiary’s dealings with the property.

issues.definition: When an apparently absolute gift is accompanied by a successive gift and restrictions that support a limited interest, the first beneficiary has a life interest.

issues.legal_issue: A donee from a life tenant cannot retain the property against the beneficiaries entitled to it after the life estate ends.
material_facts: The will gave the widow only a life estate and gave the property thereafter to other beneficiaries.
The widow gifted the property to a religious institution during her lifetime.
The widow later died, ending her life estate.
The institution claimed through the widow, and the beneficiary under the will sought possession.
issues.conclusion: The gift could not prevent the beneficiaries under the will from recovering possession after the widow’s life estate ended.
issues.legal_principle: A transferee cannot obtain a greater title than the transferor had. A gift by a life tenant cannot survive the termination of that life interest so as to defeat the remainder beneficiaries’ right to possession under the will.

rule.if: possession_claim_under_will and transferor_had_life_interest and transferee_claims_through_life_tenant and life_interest_has_ended

predicates.possession_claim_under_will: A beneficiary seeks possession on the basis of a valid testamentary gift of the property.
predicates.transferor_had_life_interest: The person who transferred the property held only a life interest under the will.
predicates.transferee_claims_through_life_tenant: The person resisting possession received the property from the life tenant.
predicates.life_interest_has_ended: The life tenant has died or the life interest has otherwise ended.

issues.definition: When a transferee claims through a life tenant whose interest has ended, the beneficiaries entitled under the will may recover possession.

issues.legal_issue: A mutation entry and a beneficiary’s failure to object when it was made do not defeat title established under a proved will.
material_facts: The will was proved and its due execution was accepted by the courts below.
The property had been mutated in the widow’s name after the testator’s death.
The beneficiary did not object to the mutation at the time, but later claimed title and possession under the will.
issues.conclusion: The mutation and the beneficiary’s failure to object to it did not extinguish the title acquired under the will or justify rejecting the will’s effect.
issues.legal_principle: A mutation entry does not by itself defeat title otherwise acquired under a will. The failure to object to a mutation is not, in the circumstances described, sufficient to discard a proved will or its effect on title.

predicates.title_dispute_based_on_proved_will: A person claims title under a will that has been proved.
predicates.mutation_recorded_in_another_person_name: An administrative mutation entry records the property in another person’s name.
predicates.beneficiary_did_not_object_to_mutation: The person claiming under the will did not challenge the mutation when it was made.

issues.definition: When title is established under a proved will, a mutation entry in another person’s name and the beneficiary’s failure to object do not defeat that title.

issues.legal_issue: A donee who does not surrender property within the time allowed under the decree may be liable for mesne profits from the specified lower appellate decree until possession is recovered.
material_facts: The court decreed recovery of possession from the donee.
It allowed the donee a period to surrender the property and held that no mesne profits would be payable if the property was surrendered within that period.

It held that if the donee did not surrender the property and execution proceedings were required, mesne profits would be payable from the date of the lower appellate court’s decree until possession was recovered, at a rate to be determined in execution.
issues.conclusion: The donee would owe no mesne profits if it surrendered the property within the allowed period; otherwise, it would be liable for mesne profits from the lower appellate decree until recovery of possession, with the rate determined by the executing court.
issues.legal_principle: The court may make liability for mesne profits conditional on whether a party complies with a possession decree within the time allowed, and may leave the rate to be determined in execution.

predicates.possession_decree_against_donee: A court orders a donee to surrender property to the person entitled to possession.
predicates.donee_fails_to_surrender_within_granted_: The donee does not surrender the property within the period allowed by the court.

issues.definition: A donee ordered to surrender property is liable for mesne profits until possession is recovered if the donee fails to surrender within the period allowed.
